extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and policy analysts studying persuasive communication (economists, political scientists, marketing researchers); also useful for practitioners interested in empirical evaluation of persuasion)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation and interpretation of persuasive communications targeted at consumers, voters, donors, and investors, including measurement (persuasion rate), identification strategies, competing models of how persuasion works, sender incentives, and equilibrium implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The persuasion rate f estimates the percentage of receivers that change behavior among those that receive a message and are not already persuaded. In a binary outcome setting with treatment group T and control group C, f = 100 * (y_T - y_C) / (e_T - e_C) / (1 - y_0) (approximate y_0 by y_C when y_0 not observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures effect on behavior (y_T - y_C) adjusted for exposure (e_T - e_C) and the remaining persuadable population (1 - y_0). If exposure in control group is small or treatment effect is small, approximating y_0 by y_C is valid. When e_T - e_C is unobserved authors sometimes assume e_T - e_C = 1, producing a lower bound. Use intent-to-treat vs actual-treatment carefully (ITT vs treatment-on-treated adjustments). Example calculations shown for GOTV, media, and advertising studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure rate (e_T - e_C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference in shares exposed to the persuasive message between treatment and control groups; a denominator component of the persuasion rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate measurement of exposure is critical: small exposure amplifies implied persuasion rates. When exposure is unobserved, assuming full exposure (100%) yields a lower bound on persuasion. Where possible measure actual exposure (e.g., diaries, ad logs, observed contacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline adoption (y_0 or y_C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The share that would adopt the behavior in absence of the message (y_0), often approximated by control-group adoption y_C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline matters because persuasion rate normalizes by the persuadable population (1 - y_0). If y_0 is high (few persuadables), small changes in y can imply large persuasion rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use randomized field experiments / credible identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer randomized assignment of exposure to measure causal effects of persuasive messages on field outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field experiments (individual-level or market-level randomization) avoid biases from nonrandom assignment and self-reported outcomes; use administrative records when possible (e.g., turnout records). Examples: GOTV field experiments, split-run advertising tests, randomized online ad exposure on Yahoo!

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit natural experiments and high-frequency variation
rubrics_metrics.description: When experiments are infeasible, use natural experiments, idiosyncratic technology adoption, timing variation, or high-frequency response windows to identify persuasion effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include staggered cable channel introductions (Fox News), local availability of a TV station (NTV in Russia), and time-stamped ad-driven calls (800 numbers) or high-frequency matched purchase/ad exposure data. Careful assumptions about exogeneity are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish belief-based vs preference-based models
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broad model classes: belief-based models where messages change receivers' beliefs (Bayesian or boundedly rational belief-updating), and preference-based models where messages affect utility directly (e.g., advertising entering utility or peripheral/emotional persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction matters for welfare implications: in standard belief-based (Bayesian) models more information cannot make receivers worse off, whereas preference-based (or non-Bayesian) channels can. Empirical testing should target predictions that separate these models (e.g., belief updating patterns, persistence, heterogeneity by prior certainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction: persuasion more effective when receivers are less certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief-based models predict persuasion is more effective when receivers have weaker priors or less experience about the object (greater uncertainty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests: compare advertising effects for inexperienced vs experienced consumers (Ackerberg on Yoplait-150); expect larger responses among those with less prior information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal contact is especially persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct, personal contact (door-to-door canvassing, personal phone calls) tends to produce substantially larger persuasion/turnout/donation effects than impersonal communications (mailers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GOTV evidence: door-to-door contact implies high persuasion rates (e.g., f ≈ 11–20%); mailers produce much smaller f (≈ 1%). Fundraising door-to-door also shows high conversion. Use these findings to design interventions when high persuasion per contact is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and partisan coverage effects (exposure-adjusted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partisan media availability can shift vote shares and attitudes; measured effects must be adjusted for exposure to compute persuasion rate (often 10–20% of the non-already-convinced audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fox News introduction, NTV in Russia, randomized newspaper subscriptions; reconcile differences in point estimates by accounting for exposure rates. Media can affect both vote choice and turnout margins—use appropriate vote-share persuasion formula when outcome is vote share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising effectiveness is mixed and context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical advertising studies (split-run tests, market-level experiments, field experiments) show mixed results: many ads have no detectable effect, while some do; results depend on experimental design and measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret observational correlations cautiously due to endogeneity of ad spending. Prefer randomized or high-frequency identification when assessing ad effectiveness. Examples include Anheuser-Busch market tests, meta-analyses finding many null results, and online large-scale randomized ad exposures with intent-to-treat and actual-exposure analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-study measures for investor-directed persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Investor responses to firm disclosures and analyst recommendations are commonly measured by event studies of stock returns around announcements, capturing marginal investor response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earnings surprises and analyst recommendation changes produce sizeable immediate returns (e.g., ± ~3% for top/bottom deciles). Most price response occurs rapidly (minutes/hours), but post-earnings announcement drift indicates continued predictable returns over subsequent quarters—consider limits to arbitrage and behavioral explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed money, gifts, and reciprocity in fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundraising evidence shows that stated seed money increases giving (inference of quality) and that small gifts included with solicitations trigger reciprocity and higher donation rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design fund-raising mailers/solicitations to include credible seed amounts or small gifts to increase take-up; be mindful that short-term gifts may not persist into future solicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogenous attention and limited demand for information
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivers choose whether and how much information to acquire; limited attention and endogenous exposure mediate persuasion effectiveness and equilibrium outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and empirical strategies should account for selection into exposure (e.g., consumers self-selecting into ad viewing) and constrained attention (limited memory, categorical thinking). This affects both estimation and welfare conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senders’ incentives and limits to distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sender incentives (advertisers, firms, analysts, media) determine the extent and direction of distortion in communications; constraints include competition, reputational concerns, third-party certification, and regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how strategic incentives (e.g., product-market competition, conflicts of interest for analysts, advertising revenues for media) interact with institutional constraints to limit or exacerbate misleading communication. Use institutional features as identification sources where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium effects and welfare depend on model and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: How persuasion affects market or political equilibria and welfare hinges on whether communication is informative or manipulative, how exposure is allocated, and on sender incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer welfare gains/losses solely from reduced measurement errors; explicitly consider whether receivers are Bayesian, boundedly rational, or subject to preference manipulation, and account for equilibrium strategic responses of senders and third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement caveats and approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Several practical measurement issues arise: (i) y_0 often unobserved and approximated by y_C, (ii) exposure in control groups may not be zero, (iii) intent-to-treat vs actual exposure differences, (iv) non-random assignment in many marketing studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report assumptions transparently, use robustness checks (e.g., assume e_T - e_C = 1 to get lower bounds), and prefer designs that observe actual exposure or exploit exogenous variation in availability/timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-response linking methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking a specific persuasive message to observed receiver action via direct response channels (response codes in ads, 800 numbers, unique URLs) enables clean measurement of ad effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use traceable response mechanisms in field settings (e.g., coded mailers, phone numbers, tracking pixels) when feasible to reduce exposure measurement error and to identify short-run causal impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate turnout vs party-switching in vote-share studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When outcome is vote share, media/messages can affect turnout and/or party switching; persuasion measures should account for both margins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specialized vote-share persuasion expression (appendix): f = (v_T - v_C) / (e_T - e_C) * (t_C t_T) / (t_0 (1 - v_0)) with approximations t_C ≈ t_0 and v_C ≈ v_0 where appropriate; carefully decompose margins in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral mechanisms: memory, double-counting, coarse thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-Bayesian behavioral channels (limited memory, double-counting repeated information, categorical or coarse thinking) can explain persistence, asymmetries, and nonstandard updating in response to persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically test for behavioral signatures (e.g., persistence beyond immediate response, over- or under-weighting of repeated messages) to distinguish from fully Bayesian belief-updating models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripheral vs central route factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological models distinguish central (informational content) from peripheral cues (emotional/heuristic elements); persuasion may operate through peripheral factors that change preferences independent of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or measures that can separate informational effects from peripheral cue effects (e.g., vary content vs pictures, vary factual information vs affective framing) to determine channels and welfare implications.
